passage:
"They said the power cut was my fault. I wasn't even home," said Yash.

"The meter is in the hall, and you were at the library," Aadhya said.

"I know. I apologised anyway. I always do."

"When did you last apologise for something that really was yours?"

Yash was quiet. "I can't remember. Something goes wrong and everyone's eyes come to me. Even my own eyes, now."

"That's your family's habit, not a fact about you."

"It feels like a fact."

"Try saying, 'This isn't mine.' Just once, at dinner."

"And then Baba goes silent for two days."

"Maybe. But you'd know that's him going quiet, not proof."

"Can I come to your study group on Sundays? I'd like somewhere else to be."

"Obviously. Bring your tea flask."

qa.q: Where was Yash when the power cut happened?
What does Yash mean by "Even my own eyes, now"?
qa.a: Yash has begun to believe the family's blame and see Yash as the cause too, feeling guilty by habit even when not at fault.

qa.q: How could Yash build support and distance from the blame?
qa.a: By joining Aadhya's Sunday study group and calmly saying "This isn't mine" when blamed unfairly.

qa.q: How might Baba react to Yash speaking up?
qa.a: Yash expects Baba to go silent for two days, which shows the family's habit of pulling back when the role is challenged.

grounding: A family blames a member for everything; the protagonist starts to see it as a family pattern, not proof of worth, and seeks outside support.

Sabina: V are you up
Vandana: yes what happened
Sabina: family dinner. my brother failed his CA exam and Ammi said it's because I "distracted him" by calling him about my job
Sabina: last month Abbu's sugar went up and apparently that was my fault too
Vandana: Sabina. girl. that's not normal
Sabina: I know it sounds bad but honestly I feel like maybe I am the problem
Sabina: I've been the problem since I was ten
Vandana: listen. when everything is always your fault, that's a pattern, not proof
Sabina: how do you know
Vandana: because I've known you eight years. you're the one who drove your dad to hospital at 2am
Sabina: 😔
Vandana: have you thought of talking to someone? a counsellor?
Sabina: my office has one
Vandana: book it. and come stay here this weekend. just to breathe
Sabina: ok. yes. thank you
Vandana: you're not the problem 🤍

qa.q: What did Ammi blame Sabina for at dinner?
qa.a: She blamed Sabina for her brother failing his CA exam.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel about being blamed?
qa.a: Sabina feels hurt and ashamed, beginning to believe she really is the problem.

qa.q: What does Vandana suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Seeing the blame as a family pattern, talking to a counsellor, and spending a weekend away help Sabina build outside support and see herself clearly.
Vandana sees her as loyal and caring, remembering how she drove her dad to hospital at 2 a.m.

grounding: A chat shows a young woman whose family blames her for everything, who begins to recognise it as a family pattern and seeks outside support and distance.

passage:
In their town near Satara, whatever went wrong in Divyansh's house was Divyansh's fault. When the buffalo fell sick, it was because he'd fed it late. When his younger brother fought at school, Divyansh should have been watching. By twenty-three he had stopped arguing. He just said sorry, automatically.

His friend Manoj, who taught at the village school, noticed. One evening at the tea stall, Divyansh apologised to the stall owner for a cup of tea that had gone cold on its own.

"Why are you sorry?" Manoj asked.

Divyansh laughed, then didn't. "Habit."

"You know it's not true, right? That it's all you?"

Divyansh stared at the road. Nobody had ever said that.

Over the next months, he started spending evenings at Manoj's, reading. He applied for a job at the sugar factory in the next town. When he moved there, the first thing he noticed was how quiet his head was.

qa.q: What did Divyansh apologise to the stall owner for?
qa.a: He apologised for a cup of tea that had gone cold on its own.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel when Manoj asked if it was all his fault?
qa.a: Divyansh felt stunned and moved, since nobody had ever questioned the blame before.

qa.q: How did Divyansh begin to see himself more clearly?
qa.a: He built outside support with Manoj, spent evenings reading, and took a job in another town for some distance.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Divyansh's automatic apologies?
qa.a: Manoj sees them as a sign that Divyansh has absorbed his family's blame, not as the truth about him.

grounding: The passage shows a young man who has absorbed the role of family scapegoat, who starts to see it as a pattern through a friend's support and builds distance to see himself clearly.
